sentences.text: Position limits concern the largest sampled absolute net position during a review period, which an endpoint forecast can miss.
We compare historical and conditional quantile forecasts using one FX market maker's positions and aggregate dealer records from the New York Fed and CFTC.
Historical rules are difficult to beat across these records, while longer-history FX gains coexist with adverse weekly outcomes and important exceptions.
Simulations, learning curves and the partly supported CFTC check are consistent with estimation costs varying with history and shrinkage, while causal attribution remains unresolved.
Practical validation should compare scores, breaches and stated limit costs against matched historical benchmarks, since different charges can favor different procedures.
Position limits concern the largest sampled absolute net position during a review period, which an endpoint forecast can miss.
We compare historical and conditional quantile forecasts using one FX market maker's positions and aggregate dealer records from the New York Fed and CFTC.
Historical rules are difficult to beat across these records, while longer-history FX gains coexist with adverse weekly outcomes and important exceptions.
Simulations, learning curves and the partly supported CFTC check are consistent with estimation costs varying with history and shrinkage, while causal attribution remains unresolved.
Practical validation should compare scores, breaches and stated limit costs against matched historical benchmarks, since different charges can favor different procedures.
Position limits must cover exposure between reviews, since a position that finishes inside a limit can still breach it earlier.
An endpoint forecast therefore answers a different question from a peak forecast, motivating comparisons on the largest sampled absolute net position.
This Treasury-bill path returns within its reported historical limit at the endpoint, although an earlier position breaches that same limit.
The example follows the earliest eligible original evaluation window, illustrating why endpoint containment can conceal exposure during the review period.
Conditional models use recent position states and calendar information to adapt a limit, but their estimated relationships consume a finite history.
A historical rule estimates fewer relationships and can remain competitive, making improvement over an explicit historical benchmark the relevant practical question.
We examine one market maker's FX record alongside two official reporting systems that describe different segments of aggregate dealer activity.
New York Fed reports cover government securities, while CFTC categories cover futures markets, requiring distinct targets, scales and historical references.
Both weekly systems report dealer aggregates rather than independent individual dealers, and their economic units and information dates remain distinct.
History, the tested penalty menu and stated limit costs organize the comparisons, while a universal history requirement and causal explanation remain unidentified.
Matched FX gains coexist with adverse weekly comparisons and reversals at the longest tested histories, keeping historical rules a demanding benchmark.
The first contribution connects simulation and FX history patterns with an additional reporting system, extending their comparison while retaining their limits.
Earlier simulations support the registered short-history and long-history loss-sign predictions, while their universal simplification claim fails and FX curves retain reversals.
The new CFTC extension agrees with the short-history counts but misses the registered long-history win target and strict-improvement target.
Its combined verdict is partial agreement, leaving the broader history pattern qualified and a universally sufficient history threshold still unestablished.
The second contribution distinguishes the amount of history from the available procedures, separating candidate performance from the effects of their selection.
An expanded penalty menu removes much of a short-history simulation loss, while financial diagnostics retain selection errors and losses within the finite menu.
The expanded menu includes an ordinary historical quantile, leaving the value of extra predictors unidentified by near-parity performance alone.
Related forecast comparisons leave historical methods alongside many uneliminated alternatives, showing why a single reported winner gives an incomplete account.
The third contribution connects forecast comparisons to stated limit costs, with reserve amounts, breach frequency and exceedance magnitude entering separately.
Their weights can change which tested report is cheaper, although local exceptions persist within the evaluated grid of hypothetical preferences.
The cost comparison illustrates this dependence on preferences, leaving realized funding gains and the effects of trading interventions outside its scope.
Matching training-label histories and refit schedules makes the benchmark explicit, while feature construction and validation can still use different information.
Causal feature effects therefore remain unidentified, and all observed failures, unavailable comparisons and inspected-period qualifications remain part of the evidence.
Section defines the response and Section reports the forecasting comparisons, separating matched conditional gains from changes in the reference procedure.
Section connects the history evidence across simulations, FX and CFTC, before Section relates these forecast comparisons to stated cost preferences.
Earlier FX studies forecast signed next-hour position intervals using historical states, calendar information and local prediction methods .
Their chronological training, calibration and test design reports scores and coverage together, providing a natural comparison for the present forecasting task.
Our peak response instead uses a complete future path segment and the current magnitude, producing different labels and limits.
Path-risk forecasts address within-period extremes, including MaxVaR's worst cumulative portfolio return under fixed holdings and diffusion assumptions .
The payment-liquidity thesis forecasts conditional maximum deficits from confidential transactions, while settlement studies examine tail liquidity needs and collateral requirements .
Duffie and colleagues study dealer capacity and Treasury-market functioning, including PnL quantile forecasts; these responses differ from the sampled absolute-position peak .
Regression quantiles target asymmetric forecast errors directly , while autoregressive quantiles and quantile forests supply other conditioning structures .
Consistent scores and elementary-score representations permit comparisons across evaluation preferences, rather than selecting a forecast solely from its apparent coverage .
The extended literature matrix compares these earlier responses with the present sampled peak, its completed labels and matched historical controls.
The matched FX gain changes interpretation with its reference, while the weekly comparisons expose both tuning errors and finite-menu losses.
Expanded simulation menus remove large short-history losses, while parameter switching misses its registered extra-loss criterion, leaving that switching effect unidentified.
Higher reserve charges and lower fixed breach charges generally favor regression in CFTC, although local exceptions remain.
Paired tests provide the statistical framework for these forecast comparisons, while inventory-sensitive quoting motivates the underlying problem of monitoring exposure .
These findings concern passive reports on observed position paths, leaving their effect on subsequent trading decisions unmeasured.

Show mean underprediction, mean overprediction and strict-breach counts together, since the unwrapped matched FX gain and daily regression exception both accompany more breaches than history.
Cost regions add reserve, breach-frequency and exceedance preferences to this joint evaluation.
FX comes from one market maker, and its original evaluation period was inspected before conditional methods were specified.
The earlier-period comparison and full-prefix backcast are retrospective, leaving a previously unseen prospective financial evaluation outside the completed evidence.
Weekly reports aggregate positions across dealers, making related categories and the CFTC survivor universe comparisons of reporting aggregates rather than independent dealer replications.
Downloaded economic-date vintages omit historical first-release information and reporting delays, keeping the retrospective position clock distinct from public information availability.
Sampled net positions can miss within-interval excursions and gross dealer exposure; daily final records are observed timestamps rather than verified market closes.
Causal effects, individual-feature effects and coverage guarantees remain unidentified by these dependent forecast comparisons, even when completed training-label histories match.
Costs illustrate fixed preferences under the recorded position paths, leaving trading returns, funding gains and institutional intervention costs unmeasured by these experiments.
Choosing the best finite candidate after evaluation is diagnostic only; validation-length and quantile-sensitivity checks are post-result analyses with numerical failures retained.
Supplement Section SID retains the original technical qualifications on simulations, aggregation and forecast comparison.
Historical rules are hard to beat in these position records.
Matched FX gains coexist with adverse daily and weekly comparisons, changing reference rankings and nonmonotone history curves.
The original evaluation period was inspected, and related reporting categories remain aggregate comparisons with individual-dealer replication outside their scope.
The history evidence supports a bounded interpretation.
Registered simulations meet the short-history and long-history loss-sign criteria, while their universal simplification claim fails.
The CFTC extension gives partial agreement: short-history disadvantage counts pass, whereas the long-history win target and strict-improvement target fail.
An automatic deployment rule based only on longer history therefore remains unsupported by these completed comparisons and their retained exceptions.
The menu and selection evidence complements that result.
A broader simulated menu reduces a large short-history disadvantage, but the available financial menu and its selection procedure still leave losses.
Access to a historical candidate leaves predictor value unidentified by menu expansion alone, since near-parity can result from selecting that historical option.
The high-quantile failures remain unavailable and prevent a general extension of the original gains to the higher target level.
Reserve amounts, breach frequency and exceedance magnitude also affect the preferred tested report under stated charges.
The fixed cost grids have local exceptions and express hypothetical preferences, rather than realized trading or funding benefits.
Validation should retain a matched historical benchmark, display the complete history sensitivity and report all three cost components alongside scores and failures.
